requirements.fact: Reflected solar radiation, tree wells, and dehydration present severe risks on sunny days.
requirements.misconception: Snow sports hazards only occur during massive blizzards or subzero deep freezes.
pamphlet_excerpts: Thermal Regulation: Layered synthetic clothing prevents sweat accumulation that causes rapid conductive body cooling.
Sun Protection: Snow reflection intensifies ultraviolet exposure requiring dark polarized sunglasses and zinc sunscreen.
Hydration Maintenance: Cold dry mountain air accelerates respiratory moisture loss requiring regular fluid intake.
Tree Wells: Deep loose snow surrounding evergreen bases causes fatal suffocation from immersion.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Participants encounter extreme ambient cold, shifting alpine weather, high altitude, and solar radiation while traveling across snow. Effective management demands continuous monitoring of weather patterns, choosing appropriate routes, and carrying emergency survival gear.
requirements.safety_callout: Stay at least ten feet away from evergreen tree trunks to avoid falling into hidden tree wells.
socratic_questions: Why does breathing dry mountain air accelerate dehydration faster than sweating during summer?
How does fresh powder under evergreen branches create an invisible trap for skiers?
What environmental clues tell your patrol that conditions require heading down immediately?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Weather Assessment: Check local avalanche forecasts and temperature trends before heading up the mountain.
Step 2 - Gear Preparation: Pack emergency shelter gear, high energy rations, spare gloves, and insulated goggles.
Step 3 - Trail Observation: Scan tree bases and steep cornice drop-offs to prevent accidental falls.
Step 4 - Group Check: Monitor patrol members continuously for pale skin, shivering, or sluggish physical movement.

sub_requirements.fact: Icy patches, wind drifts, and hidden obstacles emerge rapidly on groomed trails.
sub_requirements.misconception: Staying on marked trails completely eliminates the danger of alpine terrain hazards.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Anticipating mountain hazards involves evaluating changing weather, terrain obstacles, and trail traffic before descending. Prevention relies on proper spacing, speed control, and carrying emergency shelter supplies.

sub_requirements.fact: Rubbing damaged skin causes severe tissue loss and cellular destruction from ice crystals.
sub_requirements.misconception: Rubbing frostbitten skin with snow stimulates circulation and thaws frozen tissues safely.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Cold injuries range from frostbite and hypothermia to acute mountain sickness and severe fractures. Immediate treatment prioritizes moving the patient out of the wind, dry insulation, and gentle rewarming.

requirements.fact: Moving a patient without ski patrol sleds risks aggravating spinal and skeletal trauma.
requirements.misconception: Skiers should immediately transport injured friends down the mountain on their shoulders.
pamphlet_excerpts: Immediate Action: Rapid emergency response prevents hypothermia from worsening severe traumatic musculoskeletal injuries.
Scene Safety: Crossing skis uphill from an accident marks the site for oncoming skiers.
Patrol Contact: Ski patrol dispatchers require trail name, landmark number, and current patient condition.
Patient Warming: Insulating injured skiers from snow prevents deadly hypothermic shock during rescue waits.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Every snow sport participant must be ready to provide basic stabilization because freezing temperatures accelerate trauma complications. Prompt accident reporting to the ski patrol ensures specialized extraction toboggans and medical personnel reach the injured person.
requirements.safety_callout: Never remove an injured skier's boots on the snow because severe swelling and frostbite can occur instantly.
socratic_questions: Why does lying on frozen snow make even minor injuries life threatening?
What critical details must you give the dispatcher when reporting a mountain accident?
How do uphill warning markers prevent secondary collisions on high speed trails?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Scene Protection: Plant crossed skis uphill above the injured skier to divert approaching traffic.
Step 2 - Patient Assessment: Check responsiveness, breathing, and bleeding while protecting the spine from sudden movement.
Step 3 - Emergency Dispatch: Send two reliable companions to report the exact trail location to patrol.
Step 4 - Cold Shielding: Place dry backpacks underneath the victim to block conductive ground heat loss.

sub_requirements.fact: Witnesses must secure the scene, provide insulation, and summon professional rescuers promptly.
sub_requirements.misconception: Only certified ski patrollers have any responsibility to assist downed skiers.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Participants must maintain emergency readiness because alpine isolation delays commercial emergency medical response. Immediate buddy care shields trauma victims from rapid environmental temperature drops.

sub_requirements.fact: Contacting dispatch through phone or sending markers to lift attendants ensures rapid response.
sub_requirements.misconception: Shouting down the mountain is the standard way to summon ski patrol.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Reporting a trail incident requires delivering specific data including trail name, tower number, and injury description. Messengers should memorize exact landmarks or call the emergency dispatch number directly.

requirements.fact: Trail ratings are relative to the specific mountain terrain, not absolute across resorts.
requirements.misconception: Trail rating symbols are standardized across all ski resorts worldwide with identical steepness.
pamphlet_excerpts: Green Circle: Green circles designate easier beginner slopes with wide contours and gentle gradients.
Blue Square: Blue squares indicate more difficult intermediate terrain with moderate pitches and moguls.
Black Diamond: Black diamonds denote most difficult trails featuring steep pitches, narrow chutes, and obstacles.
Double Diamond: Double black diamonds identify expert terrain containing extreme cliff bands and hazards.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: The international trail-marking system categorizes slope difficulty using standardized geometric shapes and colors. These symbols guide participants to slopes matching their technical ability, preventing disorientation and accidents.
requirements.safety_callout: Never pass under closed trail ropes or danger signs, as unpatrolled slopes contain unmarked lethal obstacles.
socratic_questions: Why might an intermediate blue trail at a high mountain feel like a black diamond elsewhere?
What do orange hexagonal signs indicate about specialized terrain features on the slope?
How does studying the trail map at the summit prevent descending into unintended dangerous terrain?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Map Consultation: Review the resort trail map before riding lifts to identify appropriate routes.
Step 2 - Signboard Verification: Match the trail head marker shape to personal technical competence before dropping.
Step 3 - Boundary Respect: Obey orange rope closures denoting ungroomed terrain, thin cover, or avalanche closures.
Step 4 - Junction Decision: Choose lower difficulty bypass routes whenever approaching intersections with double black diamonds.

requirements.fact: Core stability and neuromuscular coordination are vital for absorbing sudden twisting forces.
requirements.misconception: Strong leg muscles alone prevent all knee injuries without any need for balance.
pamphlet_excerpts: Isometric Strength: Wall sits build quadriceps endurance needed for maintaining steady downhill athletic stances.
Core Stability: Planks strengthen abdominal muscles to maintain proper balance over shifting snow conditions.
Cardiovascular Stamina: Aerobic conditioning delays muscular exhaustion that causes late afternoon downhill ski accidents.
Dynamic Flexibility: Leg swings and hamstring stretches protect knees and hips from abrupt torque.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Snow sports demand robust muscular strength, cardiovascular endurance, and joint flexibility to withstand dynamic downhill forces. Comprehensive pre-season conditioning reduces fatigue, stabilizes connective tissues, and prevents severe knee ligament tears.
requirements.safety_callout: Stop skiing when extreme muscle fatigue sets in, because tired muscles fail to stabilize knee joints during falls.
socratic_questions: Why do the majority of alpine skiing knee injuries happen during the final runs of the day?
How does core strength help you recover balance when a ski tip catches an edge?
What specific flexibility exercises protect your knee ligaments from rotational strain?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Warmup Routine: Perform five minutes of light jumping jacks to elevate core body temperature.
Step 2 - Quadriceps Loading: Hold a ninety degree wall sit for sixty seconds to develop leg endurance.
Step 3 - Balance Training: Practice single leg squats on a balance pad to strengthen ankle stabilizers.
Step 4 - Dynamic Stretching: Complete deep lunges and torso rotations to improve hip mobility before skiing.

requirements.fact: Cotton absorbs moisture and holds it against skin, accelerating hypothermia twenty-five times faster.
requirements.misconception: Thick cotton sweatpants and hoodies provide great affordable warmth for winter snow sports.
pamphlet_excerpts: Base Layer: Synthetic or merino wool base layers pull perspiration away from cold skin.
Insulation Layer: Fleece or down mid-layers trap warm air without restricting downhill athletic motion.
Outer Shell: Waterproof breathable outer jackets block biting wind and repel freezing mountain precipitation.
Head Protection: Certified snow helmets retain head warmth while shielding skulls from high-speed impacts.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: The three-layer clothing system regulates body temperature through moisture management, thermal insulation, and weather protection. Wearing moisture-wicking base layers, fleece mid-layers, and waterproof breathable shells prevents deadly hypothermia on the mountain.
requirements.safety_callout: Ensure helmet chin straps are buckled snugly with room for only two fingers beneath the chin.
socratic_questions: Why is moisture management more critical than raw thickness when choosing winter clothing?
How do mittens keep fingers warmer than five-finger gloves in freezing conditions?
What problems occur when you wear two pairs of thick socks inside ski boots?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Base Layering: Put on moisture wicking polyester thermal underwear against the bare dry skin.
Step 2 - Thermal Stacking: Add a fleece pullover to trap body warmth around the vital organs.
Step 3 - Weather Shelling: Zip up a windproof breathable jacket over pants covering boot tops completely.
Step 4 - Extremity Coverage: Secure waterproof insulated mittens, neck gaiter, helmet, and anti-fog dual-pane goggles snugly.

requirements.fact: People ahead or downhill of you have the right of way at all times.
requirements.misconception: Skiers uphill behind you always have the right of way because they are faster.
pamphlet_excerpts: Downhill Right: Downhill skiers have the right of way because they cannot see behind.
Safe Stopping: Avoid stopping in narrow trails or where you are invisible from above.
Park Etiquette: Look before you leap to ensure landing zones are clear of fallen riders.
Avalanche Awareness: Carrying a transceiver, shovel, and probe is mandatory in snowy backcountry terrain.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Safe mountain travel requires strict adherence to Your Responsibility Code, SMART Style terrain park etiquette, and backcountry avalanche awareness. Every participant shares the duty to protect themselves and others from preventable alpine collisions and hazards.
requirements.safety_callout: Never stop in the middle of a blind trail crest or underneath terrain park jumps.
socratic_questions: Why does the person downhill always have the right of way on every trail?
How does the SMART Style system protect riders inside high-risk terrain parks?
What three pieces of rescue equipment are non-negotiable for entering avalanche terrain?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Control Maintenance: Ski at controlled speeds allowing immediate stops to avoid obstacles and people.
Step 2 - Lookout Verification: Look uphill and yield to oncoming skiers whenever merging onto a trail.
Step 3 - Park Progression: Inspect all terrain park jumps and rails before attempting any aerial maneuvers.
Step 4 - Beacon Check: Test avalanche beacon transmit and receive functions before entering any ungroomed gates.

sub_requirements.fact: The downhill skier always has right of way regardless of speed or skill.
sub_requirements.misconception: Faster skiers always have right of way over slower learners practicing downhill turns.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Your Responsibility Code outlines universal rules of conduct on ski slopes to eliminate reckless collisions. Following these rules ensures that every skier remains in control, avoids stopping in blind spots, and uses retention devices.

sub_requirements.fact: Riders must visually inspect landings and clear features before attempting jumps.
sub_requirements.misconception: Riders can jump immediately into advanced park features without inspecting landings first.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: The SMART Style program establishes safety rules specifically designed for terrain parks, pipes, and feature zones. Riders must start small, make a plan, always look, respect features, and take it easy.

sub_requirements.fact: Sidecountry gates lead to unmanaged wilderness where avalanches strike unpredictably without warning.
sub_requirements.misconception: Ski patrol bombs all backcountry peaks, making sidecountry terrain completely avalanche-proof.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Avalanche safety requires assessing snowpack stability, recognizing slope angles between thirty and forty-five degrees, and carrying rescue gear. Backcountry travelers must travel one at a time across exposed avalanche paths.

requirements.fact: Downhill ski bindings release during falls, while snowboard and snowshoe bindings stay locked.
requirements.misconception: All four snow sports disciplines share identical boot flexing and binding release mechanisms.
pamphlet_excerpts: Alpine Edge: Angling ski edges into the snowpack allows controlled turning and stopping power.
Nordic Stride: Diagonal stride combines opposite arm and leg kicks for efficient flatland propulsion.
Snowboard Carve: Shifting weight between heel and toe edges initiates fluid carving across slopes.
Snowshoe Grip: Steel crampons beneath the snowshoe deck provide traction while climbing frozen ascents.
requirements.pamphlet_summary: Scouts master technical fundamentals in one chosen discipline: downhill skiing, cross-country skiing, snowboarding, or snowshoeing. Each option requires specific equipment maintenance, balance techniques, edge control, and safe maneuvers across varied winter terrain.
requirements.safety_callout: Ensure release bindings on downhill skis are calibrated to your weight and DIN setting.
socratic_questions: How does shifting your center of gravity forward improve turning control on snow?
Why do alpine ski bindings require precision DIN settings while snowboard bindings do not?
What terrain conditions dictate choosing snowshoes over cross country touring skis?
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Gear Fitting: Adjust bindings and boot closures to ensure secure attachment without painful pinching.
Step 2 - Stance Centering: Flex knees and ankles slightly forward to maintain a centered athletic posture.
Step 3 - Edge Engagement: Apply subtle lateral pressure to roll edges into the snow for turning.
Step 4 - Controlled Deceleration: Execute a wedge, hockey stop, or toe edge slide to stop cleanly.

sub_requirements.fact: Leaning back removes ski tip control and causes dangerous high-speed runaway falls.
sub_requirements.misconception: Leaning back in your boots slows you down safely during steep downhill descents.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Alpine skiing focuses on dynamic balance, rotary motion, pressure control, and edging skills on groomed trails. Skiers master wedge christies, parallel turns, and controlled hockey stops across progressively steeper terrain.

sub_requirements.fact: Nordic boots have flexible soles and free heels to permit natural walking strides.
sub_requirements.misconception: Nordic skiers use the exact same stiff plastic boots as downhill alpine racers.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Nordic skiing incorporates diagonal strides, kick-and-glide mechanics, and uphill herringbone maneuvers across rolling winter landscapes. Equipment utilizes free-heel bindings and specialized wax or fishscale grip patterns to propel the skier.

sub_requirements.fact: Catching a downhill edge slams riders violently onto hardpack, risking wrist fractures.
sub_requirements.misconception: Catching a downhill edge is harmless because soft snow cushions all forward falls.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Snowboarding requires lateral balance, rotational body movements, and precise transitions between heel-side and toe-side edges. Riders learn safe falls, skidded traverses, and linked carved turns down novice and intermediate trails.

sub_requirements.fact: Walkers must adopt a slightly wider stance to prevent overlapping snowshoe frames.
sub_requirements.misconception: Snowshoes allow you to walk with your normal narrow city street stride.
sub_requirements.pamphlet_summary: Snowshoeing distributes body weight over a broader surface area to achieve flotation over deep unconsolidated snow. Users learn proper stride width, heel-lift ascents, step-turn maneuvers, and safe pole plant coordination.
